title: Gertrude the Great (16 November)
hook: a German nun whose visions centered on the heart of Christ

segments.voice: Yesterday, Margaret, the queen who fed orphans before she ate. Your line was first the poor.

At the Last Supper, John's Gospel gives a small, close detail: "Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved." A head resting on a chest. Close enough to hear a heartbeat. The Gospel says nothing more about it. Long afterward, a nun in a German monastery wondered about exactly that. If the beloved disciple was that close, why didn't he write down what he heard? She asked, and she wrote down the answer she received.
screen: `A HEAD ON JESUS'S CHEST.` → `CLOSE ENOUGH TO HEAR A HEARTBEAT.` → `A NUN ASKS WHY.`

segments.voice: Gertrude lived in the monastery of Helfta, in Germany, a house of women known for learning. She came there as a child and grew up among books: study, Latin, the classics. By her own account she loved them a little too much. Then, she writes, Christ came to her in a vision, gently, and she turned from a scholar who happened to pray to someone whose whole life was prayer. She wrote down what she received in a book usually called The Herald of Divine Love, and some of it her sisters wrote from what she told them. At its center is the heart of Christ. Not a symbol on a card, but a place: a home she could rest in, a fire, a fountain. In one vision, on the feast of John, she rests near the beloved disciple and asks him the question. You leaned on that chest. You heard that heart. Why did you write nothing about it? And John, in her vision, answers that his task was to speak of the Word, for the early Church. The sweetness of those heartbeats, he says, was saved for a later time, when the world had grown cold and needed warming. Some readers see in Gertrude an early voice of the devotion that Catholics later called the Sacred Heart. For her, God's love isn't only an idea. It has a pulse. Heart, in her writing, means the place where God's love and a person's love meet.
screen: `HELFTA, A HOUSE OF LEARNING.` · `FROM SCHOLAR TO A LIFE OF PRAYER.` · `THE HEART AS A HOME.` · `SAVED FOR A COLDER TIME.` · then, large: `IT HAS A PULSE.`

segments.voice: Rest a hand on your chest, find your own heartbeat, and let it set the pace for a while, no words needed. If you pray, rest there the way Gertrude pictured John resting, and let words come slowly, or not at all. If you don't, stay with the beat under your hand, the life that's been keeping time for you all along.
Gertrude. A nun of Helfta in Germany whose visions, written in The Herald of Divine Love, center on the heart of Christ.
Your line: the heart. That closes a week of saints: Luke the physician, Claret the weaver, Simon and Jude, Josaphat, Albert, Margaret, and now Gertrude. One thousand forty-three days now.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Gertrude on 16 November; Benedictine and Cistercian communities read from her writings, and some Catholics pray her prayers as part of devotion to the Sacred Heart.
